Q: How to force a transparent status bar on Samsung in Kotlin Multiplatform A:

write after the theme SongBookTheme and the background of the page will become the background of the line

enableEdgeToEdge()
ViewCompat.setOnApplyWindowInsetsListener(R.id.main) { view, insets ->
    val systemBars = insets.getInsets(WindowInsetsCompat.Type.systemBars())
    view.setPadding(systemBars.left, systemBars.top, systemBars.right, systemBars.bottom)
    insets
}

Q: Creating a non constructible object: issue with trivially copyable definition? A:

Note that =delete is not equal to "absence of" that function in that the function can still take part in overload resolution. So, using =delete on ctors for trying to create a non-constructible class isn't right, even in principle(i.e even theoretically).

For example, there are situations when the compiler won't automatically synthesize the default ctor(like if you provide a parameterized ctor). Now this absense of default ctor is what you actually want but this is not what =delete offers.

Another thing is that in your 2nd example, you're using inheritance for trying to acheive your goal(or show an example for the same) but that example is also not perfectly one-to-one with your aim because there a sub-object of type BaseImpl that gets initialized(constructed) when you wrote Concrete(int i) : BaseImpl{i}.

Q: How do I use cacerts and jks truststore together? A:

There is a very good article on the Baeldung website that addresses this question.

It appears that it is not possible to specify multiple CA certificates directly using the -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore JVM option. Only a single truststore can be configured this way.

For us, the fastest and simplest solution was to add our custom CA certificates to the default JRE cacerts truststore.

By doing this, our application was able to connect to:

  • internal servers using self-signed or private CA certificates, and
  • public internet servers signed by well-known public CAs.

Example using keytool:

You can import a custom CA certificate into the default truststore using the official keytool utility:

keytool -importcert \
  -cacerts \
  -storepass changeit \
  -alias my-root-ca \
  -file ROOT-CA.cer

Notes:

  • The default password for cacerts is changeit (unless it has been changed).
  • The -cacerts option for -importcert is supported only in JDK/JRE 9 and later.
  • For Java 8 and earlier, you must explicitly specify the keystore path using -keystore: 
    -keystore $JAVA_HOME/jre/lib/security/cacerts

Further techniques:

The referenced article show other ways to do it: adding the extra trust store programmatically, but this is quite more complex. In general if you use containers, you can always build easily a new image with your updated certificate(s) independently of your software release.

Q: Creating a non constructible object: shouldn't std::bit_cast be constrained to implicit lifetime types? A:

The key point is that C++ gives trivially copyable types a special rule: their lifetime can begin simply by reading or copying their bytes. No constructor call is required. This is why std::bit_cast only checks for trivial copyability and not implicit‑lifetime status.

Your class deletes all constructors, but it still has a trivial assignment operator and no non‑trivial members. That makes it trivially copyable, and trivially copyable types are allowed to be materialized from raw storage. The standard treats the act of reading those bytes as enough to create the object.

So even though the class design suggests “you shouldn’t be able to make one of these,” the language rules say otherwise. The type system gives you no way to block object creation if the type is trivially copyable.
